questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a founding charter transferred
questions.learningObjective: state the design principle of a collective security charter
questions.stem: After a world war fifty-one governments signed a charter whose stated purpose is to make an armed attack a matter for a collective decision rather than a private response, and the charter creates no force of its own. Which feature of that design does the most to explain the intent?

options.text: Responsibility passes to a body where the state that was attacked cannot act on its own
The absence of any force shows the founders expected aggression to have ended for good
options.misconception: reads a mechanism gap as confidence in the future

options.text: Fifty-one signatures show that every government in the world had joined the arrangement
options.misconception: counts signatories as though they were all states

options.text: Saying nothing about force means members intended to act only if the aggressor agreed with them
options.misconception: treats silence in a charter as a requirement of the other side's consent

questions.explanation: The design moves the decision away from the injured state, which is the whole point, since a state that has been attacked will want an answer that harms the attacker, and a body in which others also hold a vote forces the response to be chosen rather than merely carried out. That is what the transfer of responsibility achieves, and it explains why the absence of a force is not an oversight: the body is a place for deciding, not for fighting. The distractors each read a structural gap as optimism, or treat a signature list and a silence as carrying meanings they do not.
questions.hint: Ask what an attacked state would want a response to be, and who else must agree to it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rule that protects the seats it names
questions.learningObjective: explain how an amendment rule can lock in the position of its own beneficiaries
questions.stem: A body's written rules require any change to those rules to pass a two-thirds majority of the members and, in addition, the concurring vote of every permanent member, and no seat can be added or removed except by that same procedure. Which feature does the rule protect?

options.text: The permanent members' position, since each of them can refuse the body's own amendment
Amendments are made only by agreement, since a concurring vote is required to pass them
options.misconception: treats a handful of concurring votes as though all members had to agree

options.text: Every member holds an equal veto, since the majority threshold can always be withheld
options.misconception: reads a voting threshold as a veto belonging to each member

options.text: The permanent members may enlarge their own number whenever they agree among themselves
options.misconception: reverses who may change the rule about the seats

questions.explanation: The rule does two things at once: it makes ordinary change possible by ordinary majority, and it makes change to the composition of the privileged group require the agreement of that group, which is a self-locking arrangement. A member outside it therefore faces the same prospect the permanent members would if they were a minority, which is the difficulty a reform proposal runs into. The distractors each misread the mechanism, two of them by treating a threshold as a veto and one by reversing who the rule binds.
questions.hint: Ask who can block a change to the list of members who can block changes.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A resolution with nothing behind it
questions.learningObjective: identify the exact step at which a collective body cannot proceed
questions.stem: An assembly of states resolves that an aggressor must withdraw, and a council is asked to recommend what members should do about it, but the charter creates no force and no duty to carry out a recommendation. Which feature best explains the consequence?

options.text: A decision is separated from any means of carrying it out, so a resolution can stand without being implemented
The absence of any duty to comply means members were free to deny that the body existed at all
options.misconception: turns a gap in enforcement into a denial of the body's standing

options.text: The lack of a force shows the members had agreed among themselves that war would not recur
options.misconception: reads a missing mechanism as a shared confidence

options.text: Because only recommendations are made, no member can ever be judged in the wrong
options.misconception: converts a weakness in the system into a protection for members

questions.explanation: A resolution is a statement of what ought to happen, and implementing it requires somebody with a duty and a means, and this arrangement provides neither, so the failure is not a matter of will but of the last step in the chain. That is why the body can hold a debate, vote and be entirely unable to act, and why the gap is visible in the charter rather than in any later failure of nerve. Each distractor converts the missing step into a different thing, from indifference to confidence to immunity.
questions.hint: Ask who is obliged to do anything after the vote, and with what means.

questions.topic: What a mandate's class decides
questions.learningObjective: identify what a classification of territory governs
questions.stem: Under a mandate the administering power is told which of three classes of territory it has been given, and the class assigned to a territory is what fixes how much administration the administrator is expected to provide there. Which statement about the classification is soundest?

options.text: The class sets the level of administration expected, so one rule yields different duties in different territories
The class decides whose views must be sought before the territory's future is settled
options.misconception: attaches the class to a rule about consultation the statement does not give

options.text: The class ranks the territory's importance, so the highest class went to the richest land
options.misconception: reads a statement about development as a ranking of value

options.text: The class fixes the length of the mandate, so a higher class always carried a longer term
options.misconception: confuses a category of territory with a term of years

questions.explanation: The classification works as a scale of duties, since it is set by reference to what the territory is judged ready for, and a single rule then means different obligations in different places depending on which class each was assigned. That is what makes the classification operative rather than descriptive: it changes what the administrator must do, not only how outsiders describe it. Each distractor attaches the class to a function it does not carry, whether consultation, value or duration.
questions.hint: Ask what an administrator must do differently once a territory is in a different class.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: One principle, two territories, two records
questions.learningObjective: weigh the same principle applied where evidence is present and absent
questions.stem: A memorandum argues that a principle requires authority to pass to the people of a territory, and it is used in support of a transfer in one case. A commission sent to a second territory reports that no comparable expression of a wish exists there, and the principle is not applied. Which statement is the safest about the pair?

options.text: The same test was applied in one case and found absent in the other, so what differs is the evidence and its weighing
The second case shows the principle was never binding on any state at all
options.misconception: infers that a principle is void because it was applied unevenly

options.text: The commission's report proves that the people of the second territory did not want the change
options.misconception: treats the absence of a recorded wish as a recorded refusal

options.text: The memorandum shows the first case was decided by the same commission that visited the second
options.misconception: invents a common authorship for two separate acts

questions.explanation: A principle applied to two cases produces a comparison, and the comparison here turns on what each record contains, since one is supported by a stated test applied to a recorded wish and the other by a finding that no such record exists. Naming that difference stops short of a verdict about the principle itself, which would require a wider record, and stops short of a verdict about the second territory's inhabitants, which the commission's silence cannot supply. The distractors each turn uneven application into nullity, absence of evidence into evidence of refusal, or two documents into one author.
questions.hint: Ask what each record contains, and what silence in a record can show.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A sanctions regime and the step it lacks
questions.learningObjective: locate the missing step in a monitoring-and-recommendation system
questions.stem: A sanctions regime lists what members may not do, creates a committee to examine what is being done, and may recommend that members act, but it can neither inspect a member nor punish one that ignores the list. Which feature best explains the gap?

options.text: Monitoring and recommendation exist while compulsion does not, so compliance rests on members' own willingness
Without inspection the committee's findings must be unreliable, since nothing checks them
options.misconception: treats absent verification as proof that reports are false

options.text: A list of prohibitions is void, since no body was given power to enforce it
options.misconception: announces a legal nullity the regime's own text does not imply

options.text: The regime must lapse, because a regime that cannot be enforced cannot be renewed
options.misconception: predicts the end of a system from a feature it has always had

questions.explanation: The regime contains every part of an enforcement system except the last one, since it can name conduct, gather information about it and recommend a response, and what it cannot do is make a member comply, so the whole structure depends on members deciding to act on a recommendation addressed to them. That is a specific and diagnosable weakness, and it explains both why the list can grow elaborate and why it can be ignored. The distractors each convert a missing step into a defect in the evidence, in the law, or in the system's continuation.
questions.hint: Ask what the last step in an enforcement chain would be, and whether it is here.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The refusal that suspended a guarantee
questions.learningObjective: explain how a guarantee can fail at its decision step
questions.stem: A system of states promises that an attack on a member will be met by the others, and its rule requires the others to reach a decision before any of them acts; when a member is attacked they confer and then take nothing, and the system is not again used for the purpose it was made. Which feature best explains the collapse?

options.text: The guarantee ran through a decision the members could decline to take, so one refusal suspended the arrangement
The members' forces were too small, so the system was never capable of working as designed
options.misconception: substitutes a question of resources for the rule described

options.text: The system worked as intended, since it revealed which members would not fight
options.misconception: reads a collapse as a successful test

options.text: The attack showed the rule was unlawful, so the arrangement was void from its first day
options.misconception: invents a legal invalidation to explain a political failure

questions.explanation: A promise that is implemented by a meeting is a promise whose performance depends on attendance, and once the members have shown they will confer and then stop, the mechanism that was supposed to produce action has produced its opposite, and there is nothing in the arrangement that compels a second attempt. That is a failure at the decision step, which is a different diagnosis from a shortage of means or a shortage of will, and it is the one the record supports. The distractors each substitute a different failure, and one of them praises the outcome.
questions.hint: Ask what the members had to do before the guarantee produced anything.

questions.topic: The decision a settlement postponed
questions.learningObjective: identify what an agreed settlement defers rather than settles
questions.stem: In 1938 a government signed an agreement that removed territory from its own map, and its leader then said publicly that the question of that border had been settled for the time being. Which statement best describes the decision the agreement deferred?

options.text: Whether to take the risk of a war the government had concluded it was not ready to win
How the remaining territory should be administered, since the agreement settled only borders
options.misconception: reduces the agreement to a boundary and invents an administrative question

options.text: Whether the other signatory would keep its own promises, since the agreement bound one side only
options.misconception: asserts a one-sided instrument the record does not describe

options.text: Where the border actually ran, since the parties disagreed about the line itself
options.misconception: supplies a surveying dispute the transfer of territory does not require

questions.explanation: A transfer of territory purchased with public reassurance is a payment for postponing a decision, and the decision being postponed is the one the payer judged it could not survive, which is a statement about a government's own assessment of its position rather than about anybody's character. The phrase for the time being is the checkable part, since it records that the settlement was understood as provisional by the party that proclaimed it. The distractors each find a different question left open, none of which the agreement's subject matter requires.
questions.hint: Ask what a signatory buys by agreeing now rather than later, and what it admits about its own strength.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A commitment without a decision procedure
questions.learningObjective: state what a pact obliges and what it leaves to judgement
questions.stem: A pact provides that an armed attack on one signatory is to be treated as an attack on all of them, and it names no procedure for deciding whether an attack has taken place or who began it. Which feature does that combination create?

options.text: A commitment in form, with the judgement about the attack left to the signatories themselves
A commitment that cannot be invoked, since a pact naming no procedure creates no obligation
options.misconception: converts the absence of a procedure into the absence of a duty

options.text: A commitment that binds only the signatory whose territory has been attacked
options.misconception: narrows an obligation running to all members into one for the victim only

options.text: A commitment that each signatory may set aside once a war has actually begun
options.misconception: invents a right of withdrawal the text does not contain

questions.explanation: The pact says what must follow if an attack occurs and leaves open the question of whether one has, and that question has to be settled by the members, which is what gives each of them a moment at which the commitment can be argued into or out of use. A rule without a procedure is not a rule without force; it is a rule whose application is contested. The distractors each remove the commitment, narrow it to one member, or grant a discretion the text does not give.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be decided before the commitment can operate, and who decides it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Aid released against completed work
questions.learningObjective: explain what instalment release does to the control of a reconstruction programme
questions.stem: A reconstruction programme draws up an agreed list of projects, releases money as each project is certified complete, and requires the recipient government to provide a share of the cost in its own currency. Which feature of that design does the most work?

options.text: Payment is tied to finished work, so the programme can be changed as the situation in the country changes
Every project is fixed at the start, so nothing can be altered as conditions change
options.misconception: reads a list of projects as a prohibition on revising them

options.text: The recipient's own contribution is eliminated, since the money arrives in foreign currency
options.misconception: treats a co-financing requirement as though it were absent

options.text: The programme requires repayment in the currency the country earns from exports
options.misconception: supplies a repayment clause the design does not mention

questions.explanation: Releasing money against completed work puts the funder in the position of deciding again at every instalment, and that is what converts a fixed plan into something revisable, since a project that is going badly can be reprioritised before the balance is paid. questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a peg obliges a central bank to do
questions.learningObjective: state the standing obligation created by a fixed rate
questions.stem: Under a system of pegged rates each government fixes its currency's value against another and undertakes to buy or sell at that figure for as long as the system lasts. Which feature of the system does that undertaking carry?

options.text: The promise is unconditional, so defending the figure draws on reserves rather than on argument
The figure may be abandoned whenever reserves run short, since a peg is only a target
options.misconception: reads an undertaking as an aspiration with no commitment

options.text: The peg fixes the rate between the members and leaves every other pairing free to move
options.misconception: mistakes a member's undertaking as a network of fixed rates

options.text: Any member may leave the system, since pegging was optional from the first day
options.misconception: supplies a standing release that joining a system does not give

questions.explanation: A peg is a promise about the future made in the present, and the cost of keeping it falls whenever private holders of the currency want to sell more of it than buyers want, which is a cost the central bank pays in reserves and cannot avoid by argument. The undertaking is what makes the rate credible to holders of the currency, and it is also what makes the position hard to leave, since leaving is a visible event. The distractors each soften the promise, add a network of rates, or grant a release the system does not contain.
questions.hint: Ask who pays when private sellers outnumber private buyers at the fixed figure.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The month a defence ran out of reserves
questions.learningObjective: explain what a currency crisis shows about a standing rate commitment
questions.stem: A government holds a fixed figure for years by selling reserves; in one month sellers demand more currency than its reserves can supply, it stops defending the figure, and the rate moves sharply. Which feature of the episode best explains what it shows?

options.text: A fixed rate is a standing obligation, and the defence ends when the means to sustain it are gone
The rate moved because the government had secretly reduced the figure months earlier
options.misconception: replaces a documented failure with a hidden one the record does not show

options.text: The episode shows fixed rates are stronger than floating ones, since they lasted for years
options.misconception: reads a long defence and a sharp break as a general ranking of systems

options.text: The government could not buy reserves, since a member may not hold foreign currency
options.misconception: asserts a prohibition the premise of selling reserves contradicts

questions.explanation: The episode is an exhaustion rather than a surprise, because defending a figure means meeting every offer to sell, and the limit arrives when the reserves that make that possible run below what is being asked for, at which point there is no version of the policy left to follow. That makes the fixed rate a promise with a balance sheet attached, which is why the same system can hold for years and then fail in a month. The distractors each substitute a hidden decision, a general verdict on systems, or a prohibition the premises contradict.
questions.hint: Ask what the government had to do every day the rate was held, and what happens when it can no longer do it.

questions.topic: Why an outer integration step needs the inner one
questions.learningObjective: sequence integration stages by what each requires of the previous
questions.stem: A regional project passes from a free trade area to a customs union and then to a common market, and the members treat the order as one in which each step needs the one before it. Which feature best explains the sequence?

options.text: Without a common external rate, removing internal duties lets goods enter through the least protected member and come back out again
Each step was required by an older institution that all the members had already joined
options.misconception: invents an external requirement the project did not need

options.text: The stages were separated by fixed years written into the founding agreement
options.misconception: supplies a timetable where the constraint was structural

options.text: The customs union came first, and the free trade area was added afterwards at the request of smaller members
options.misconception: reverses the sequence the project followed

questions.topic: Power exercised through approval of national plans
questions.learningObjective: explain how a joint authority gains control over a national decision
questions.stem: A joint authority is given power over a river on which every member depends, may approve or reject each member's plan for drawing water from it, and a member that builds a scheme without approval loses its use of the water. Which feature is doing the work?

options.text: Approval of national plans puts a shared resource under a common control without a common owner of it
The loss of access is a penalty, so the arrangement is judicial rather than administrative
options.misconception: classifies a sanction for unauthorised use as a court judgement

options.text: The authority's power is direct, since it operates the works itself in every member state
options.misconception: claims ownership of the works the approval mechanism leaves with members

options.text: The members keep full control, since an approval is advice that a member may always ignore
options.misconception: treats a condition on access as though it carried no consequence

questions.topic: Two courts and the difference in consequence
questions.learningObjective: state what distinguishes a constitutional court from an ordinary court
questions.stem: A constitutional court is asked whether a statute is consistent with the constitution, declares it void, and the government complies. On the same facts the ordinary courts could only have recorded a view for the government to weigh. Which feature distinguishes the two?

options.text: One can remove a law from force while the other can only state an opinion, so the difference is in what follows
One hears cases that turn on the constitution while the other hears disputes between private parties
options.misconception: describes subject matter, which both courts share in practice

options.text: One holds its office for a fixed term while the other serves during good behaviour
options.misconception: supplies a tenure difference that the account does not mention

options.text: One hears appeals from the other while the other hears cases in the first instance

The common currency failed, since a currency cannot outlive the union that issued it
options.misconception: makes a monetary arrangement the cause of a political withdrawal

questions.learningObjective: identify the conflict between two elements of a reform package
questions.stem: In a state where one party directs the economy, prices have been fixed for years and a queue has formed outside a shop. The party's economic officials propose removing the controls on goods while keeping the price ceilings. Which statement best describes the difficulty they face?

Removing the controls needs a parliamentary majority the party does not hold

options.misconception: reads a demand-side queue as evidence of an output shortage

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: An institution that can decide and cannot act
questions.learningObjective: explain how an institution's authority can exceed its capacity in a crisis
questions.stem: Explain how a body created by agreement among states can hold wide powers on paper and still be unable to act in a crisis, and name the three features of its rules that produce the gap.

answer.exemplar: An institution created by agreement draws its authority from the consent of its members, and that is also the limit on it, so a body can be given the power to name a breach, condemn it and require a report, and then discover that the next step belongs to somebody else. Three features of the rules produce the gap, and they work together rather than separately. The first is a deliberative requirement: the body acts only after its members meet and decide, which converts urgency into calendar time and means the interval between a crisis beginning and the body speaking belongs to no institution. The second is a blocking power, which is worth most before anyone has voted, so a member who expects to be outvoted can prevent a vote altogether and the sensible response is to keep talking. The third is the absence of any means, since a resolution requires somebody with a duty and an instrument to carry it out, and a body created by consent has neither the duty nor the instrument. The order in which these bite matters, because the deliberative rule is what creates the delay and the blocking power is what makes the delay the only sensible option, while the missing means is what makes the eventual result inert. A useful check on the whole diagnosis is that such a body is often strong where its members agree and weak precisely where they do not, and a crisis is by definition a place where they do not. That is also why an institution with an impressive list of powers can be less capable in an emergency than a smaller body with fewer powers and a standing force, and why the correct question about any such arrangement is not how much it may do but how many people must agree before it does anything at all.

The second is a blocking power, which is worth most before anyone has voted, so a member who expects to be outvoted can prevent a vote altogether and the sensible response is to keep talking. The third is the absence of any means, since a resolution requires somebody with a duty and an instrument to carry it out, and a body created by consent has neither the duty nor the instrument. The order in which these bite matters, because the deliberative rule is what creates the delay and the blocking power is what makes the delay the only sensible option, while the missing means is what makes the eventual result inert. A useful check on the whole diagnosis is that such a body is often strong where its members agree and weak precisely where they do not, and a crisis is by definition a place where they do not. That is also why an institution with an impressive list of powers can be less capable in an emergency than a smaller body with fewer powers and a standing force, and why the correct question about any such arrangement is not how much it may do but how many people must agree before it does anything at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the paper says the body may do, and what it must wait for before it begins.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two instruments surrendered, many retained
questions.learningObjective: explain how a currency union removes some levers and leaves others
questions.stem: Explain what a member gives up when it joins a currency union, why the adjustment problems it then faces arrive in the form they do, and which instruments remain available to it.

answer.exemplar: A member gives up two instruments, the rate of interest and the exchange rate, and the reason is structural rather than legalistic: both are set for an area larger than any single member, and a member that could still move its own would withdraw from the agreement the fact of using it, so the union holds only because the individual move is unavailable. What remains is everything a government can do through its own budget, its own taxes, its own labour law and its own spending, and that list is longer than it first appears and slower in operation. The asymmetry is the whole difficulty, because the surrendered instruments work in hours and the retained ones work through legislation and bargaining over years, so a shock arrives at the pace of money while the adjustment has to run at the pace of politics. That is why a member's trouble so often appears as unemployment in one region rather than as a currency crisis it can resolve, since a currency is no longer available to it as a remedy, and wages are the last price to fall and the first number a government is judged on. The recurring proposals to move monetary authority to a level above the union follow from the same logic, since a member that cannot set a rate can still ask for the rule that sets it to be changed, which is a slower and far less certain route to the same relief. What the union does not remove is responsibility: a member that has surrendered an instrument has not been relieved of the consequences of the shocks that arrive while it holds one, and the discipline of the arrangement lies in whether it can reach the remaining instruments in time.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: More goods and a wider gap
questions.learningObjective: explain how freeing prices can raise output and widen inequality at once
questions.stem: Explain how a government can free prices and trade, see output rise, and also see the gap between the richest and the rest widen, and say which part of the same process does each thing.

answer.exemplar: The two results come from different parts of one process, and separating them is the whole explanation. Output rises because a price that has been fixed for years is a price that carries no information, and while it stands a producer cannot tell whether a shortage is a shortage of buyers or a shortage of goods, so investment goes into the goods that were planned rather than the ones wanted. Freeing the price replaces an administrative guess with a signal, and buyers can find what they want instead of taking what was produced, which raises output without anyone's share being cut. The widening gap comes from the same opening acting on the supply side, where a firm that was protected by a plan or a tariff can now fail against an import, and failure is a concentrated event: one employer, one district, one wage that stops rising while every other price is moving. The gain from cheaper goods arrives in small amounts to everyone who shops, and the loss arrives in full to a few thousand people at one gate, so an arithmetic of small gains and large losses widens the distribution without anyone having intended it. A third contribution is institutional rather than arithmetic, since private credit, land and schooling respond to the new returns long before public provision can move, so those who can buy their way to a good school do so while the state system still reflects the old distribution. None of this makes the freeing of prices a mistake, and it is worth saying why: the counterfactual in which the price is not freed is a queue rather than a cheaper shop. But it does locate the costs, and a government that wants both aims has to build the compensation before it lifts the ceiling rather than after the district's wages have already been set fifteen years below the national average.
